newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine interest rates likely to stay high.
newsitem.headline: Philippine interest rates likely to stay high.

text.p: The Philippines' move to take the heat off the peso will lead to an easing of interest rates but probably not fast enough to avoid higher inflation in the short term, analysts said on Monday.

"Everybody agrees this (the high rates) is temporary. But you can never tell if there is a second or third wave of attacks," a bank economist said, noting de facto devaluations of the Thai baht and peso had also hit the Malaysian ringgit and the Indonesian rupiah.

"We expect the central bank to be prudent in bringing down the interest rate. You still have to stabilise the economy to contain inflationary pressures," said Jose Mario Cuyegeng, research director of ING Barings Securities.
The Philippine central bank on Friday said it would allow the peso to move in a new, wider range, hoping speculation would fizzle out enough to allow its its key rate to finally settle down.
The central bank raised its closely watched overnight borrowing rate last week to a 2-1/2 year high of 32 percent to ward off speculation.

The central bank overnight borrowing rate reached a year-low of 9.9 percent in April before peso came under pressure. On a worst case scenario, inflation could shoot up by close to 10 percent because of the central bank's looser grip on the peso, Cuyegeng said.
The weaker peso, which touched a four-year low of 29.75 to the dollar on Monday, may trigger increases in power rates, oil prices and possibly wages.
That could keep the benchmark 91-day T-bill rate at around 13 percent for the rest of the year, he said.
On Monday, the 91-day rate climbed to a two-year high of 13.217 percent from last week's 12.175 percent.
Lito Dalit, economist at AsianBank, said he expected the 91-day rate to average 11.8 percent, exceeding his original forecast of 11 percent but still below last year's average of 12.4 percent.
The rate so far this year has averaged 10.546 percent because of low interest rates in the first five months.
Volatility in the exchange rate and price increases in the second half of the year would push the 91-day rate higher, he said.

Though inflation could jump to nine percent by year-end, the economy is still poised to achieve its six to 6.5 percent inflation target for the year, Dalit said. Inflation averaged at 4.6 percent in the first half.
